summary:
West Kalimantan records no separate LGBTI legislation or enforcement, so the national framework of Indonesia governs what a visitor faces, and no sub-national divergence is documented in the sources.

Indonesia's penal code, signed in December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026, penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Indonesian law provides no explicit protection of transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Constitution does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a conservative petition 5-4 that had sought to criminalise homosexuality and extra-marital sex, declining to add them to the Penal Code.

Violence against trans people is documented at national scale. Between 14 and 16 July 2026 vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia. In Bogor, more than fifteen trans women were doused, stripped and beaten, and footage of the attacks was shared online.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats, alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction.

A trans traveller has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Peruvian Harvard student and trans activist, was arrested on drug charges at an Indonesian airport in 2022 while on honeymoon. During a call his mother was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release; he died in custody. She alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Venue raids are a documented enforcement route. On 22 June 2025 police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called the operation a violation of human rights and privacy.

Legal gender recognition is demanding: changing gender markers on documents requires sex reassignment surgery plus judicial approval.
tangentialFactors:
Two provinces add a layer of their own. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, and in Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. West Kalimantan has no equivalent provision.

A researcher cited in August 2026 reporting documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the October 2025 decree moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy, and reporting from the same month ties that framing to the wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women.

Provincial moral laws remain part of the enforcement texture alongside the national penal code, so a visitor crossing provincial boundaries moves between different moral-law regimes even where the national provisions apply everywhere.
localsOnly:
Transgender Indonesians who do not hide their identity often struggle to keep legitimate employment and can be pushed into sex work.

A global survey reports that discrimination and harassment are not uncommon among LGBTI Indonesians, though direct violence is recorded as rare outside the documented episodes.

Legal gender change requires sex reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, a process that residents of West Kalimantan share with all Indonesians.

West Kalimantan itself records no separate LGBTI legislation or enforcement, so residents live under the same national moral-law provisions, the same constitutional silence on gender identity, and the same security framing applied to visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
West Kalimantan-specific enforcement is unresolved. The sources contain no reporting on police conduct, raids, arrests or prosecutions within this province, and whether the national penal code provisions have been applied here is not stated.

Whether the 14-16 July 2026 vigilante wave included attacks inside West Kalimantan is not documented; the only named incident in the sources occurred in Bogor.

No sourced information covers access to gender-affirming care, HIV services or safe venues in West Kalimantan. Entry and visa screening practices that might reveal a visitor's gender history or documents are likewise not documented in the sources.
